# Cause of the inconsistency

The alias/rewrite from old `seaborn-*` names to the new `seaborn-v0_8-*` names
lives **only inside `matplotlib.style.core.use()`**, in its local helper
function `fix_style()`:

```python
def fix_style(s):
    if isinstance(s, str):
        s = style_alias.get(s, s)
        if s in [
            "seaborn", "seaborn-bright", "seaborn-colorblind", ...
        ]:
            _api.warn_deprecated(...)   # the deprecation warning users see
            s = s.replace("seaborn", "seaborn-v0_8")
    return s

for style in map(fix_style, styles):
    ...
    elif style in library:
        _apply_style(library[style])
```

`use()` maps every requested style name through `fix_style` *before* looking
it up, so `'seaborn-colorblind'` silently becomes `'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'`,
which really does exist in `library` (the dict built from the files under
`lib/matplotlib/mpl-data/stylelib/`, which were renamed to the
`seaborn-v0_8-*` naming scheme). That's why `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')`
works and prints the deprecation message.

`plt.style.library`, however, is just the plain dictionary populated by
`update_user_library`/`read_style_directory` when the module is imported (and
refreshed by `reload_library()`). It only ever contains the *actual* file-based
keys (`'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'`, etc.) and `'default'`/`'classic'`-type
built-ins. There is no alias entry, alias-generating code, or `__getitem__`
override anywhere that inserts the legacy `'seaborn-colorblind'` name (or any
of the other old `seaborn-*` names) into `library`. The rewriting logic in
`fix_style()` is private to the `use()` function and is never applied to, or
reflected in, the `library` mapping itself.

# Conclusion

The inconsistency is caused by **`fix_style()` inside `matplotlib.style.core.use()`**,
which performs the "seaborn" → "seaborn-v0_8" name translation (and emits the
deprecation warning) only for names passed through `style.use()`. The
`style.library` dictionary is populated independently by
`update_user_library`/`read_style_directory` and has no knowledge of this
alias table, so it never contains the deprecated bare `seaborn-*` keys.
Because the alias mapping is not applied when building/exposing `library`,
directly indexing `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` raises
`KeyError`, even though `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')` succeeds by
silently rewriting the name to `'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'` before looking it
up. In short: the alias resolution exists in exactly one place (`use()`'s
local `fix_style` closure) and is not shared with, or exposed through,
`style.library`, producing two different behaviors for what looks like the
same style name.

results.finishSummary: The old-seaborn-name aliasing (e.g. 'seaborn-colorblind' -> 'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind') is implemented only as a private string-substitution inside style.use()'s fix_style() helper, not as an actual/alias entry in the style.library dict, so direct dict lookups on library bypass the translation and raise KeyError even though use() works.

# Why `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')` works but `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` raises `KeyError`

## Root cause

The alias/rename logic for the old "seaborn-*" style names lives **only inside
`matplotlib.style.core.use()`**, in its inner helper function `fix_style()`
(lib/matplotlib/style/core.py, around lines ~113-142):

```python
def fix_style(s):
    if isinstance(s, str):
        s = style_alias.get(s, s)
        if s in [
            "seaborn", "seaborn-bright", "seaborn-colorblind", ...
        ]:
            _api.warn_deprecated(...)
            s = s.replace("seaborn", "seaborn-v0_8")
    return s

for style in map(fix_style, styles):
    ...
```

When you call `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')`, the name is first passed
through `fix_style`, which:

1. Detects that the string is one of the old, no-longer-shipped
   `"seaborn-*"` names (matched against a hard-coded list of the 16 original
   names).
2. Emits the deprecation warning.
3. Rewrites the string in place, turning `"seaborn-colorblind"` into
   `"seaborn-v0_8-colorblind"` — the *actual* key that now exists in
   `style.library` (because the style files themselves were renamed/moved to
   `seaborn-v0_8-*.mplstyle`, and `style.library` is only ever populated with
   those new file-derived names).
4. Only *after* this rewriting does `use()` look the name up
   (`style in library`) and apply it.

So `use()` never actually looks up `'seaborn-colorblind'` in `library` — it
silently substitutes `'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'` first and looks that up
instead.

`plt.style.library`, on the other hand, is a plain dict
(`matplotlib.style.core.library`) populated once at import time by
`update_user_library()` / `reload_library()` by scanning the on-disk
`stylelib` directories for `*.mplstyle` files and by iterating
`matplotlib.style.core._base_library`. Since the actual shipped files are now
named `seaborn-v0_8-*.mplstyle` (the old `seaborn-*.mplstyle` files were
removed/renamed as part of the 3.6 deprecation), the dict never contains a key
called `'seaborn-colorblind'` at all — only `'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'`.
Indexing `library['seaborn-colorblind']` therefore raises `KeyError`.

## The inconsistency / bug

The renaming/alias mechanism (the hard-coded list of old names plus the
`.replace("seaborn", "seaborn-v0_8")` substitution) is implemented as a
**local side effect inside `use()`'s `fix_style()` closure**, rather than as
part of the `library` dict itself (e.g. via `library.__missing__`,
`__getitem__` override, or by populating `library` with backward-compatible
aliases pointing to the same rc dict). Because the alias-resolution logic is
private to `use()`, any other consumer of `style.library` — including simply
indexing it directly as `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']`, or code
that iterates/looks up names some other way — does not get the benefit of the
alias translation and instead sees a plain `KeyError`, even though the
"same" style name works fine through `style.use()`.

In short: **the deprecated-name → new-name aliasing for the old seaborn
styles is a one-off string-rewrite hidden in `style.use()`'s `fix_style`
helper, not a genuine entry (or alias) in the `style.library` mapping, so
`use('seaborn-colorblind')` and `library['seaborn-colorblind']` are
inconsistent: only the former goes through the translation step.**

results.finishSummary: The bug is in Media.merge in django/forms/widgets.py: it does pairwise, order-dependent list-splicing (using a single last_insert_index cursor) instead of building a full constraint graph and topologically sorting it, so it both raises a false MediaOrderConflictWarning (comparing accidental positions rather than real stated constraints) and produces a final combined order that violates FancyTextWidget's real ordering constraint.

# Answer

## Responsible function

`django.forms.widgets.Media.merge` (a `@staticmethod` on `Media`, around line 118
of `django/forms/widgets.py`). This is the function called (pairwise, via
`Media.__add__`/`media_property`) to combine every widget's `Media.js`/`Media.css`
list into the form's overall media list, and it is exactly what produces the
spurious `MediaOrderConflictWarning` and the wrong final ordering described in
the question.

## Reproducing the bug

Combining the three widgets happens as a series of pairwise merges:

```
merge(['color-picker.js'], ['text-editor.js'])
    -> ['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']          # step 1

merge(['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js'],
      ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js'])
    -> ['text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']   # step 2
    -> also raises: "Detected duplicate Media files in an opposite order:
                     text-editor-extras.js
                     text-editor.js"
```

This is wrong on two counts:
* The warning is bogus: `FancyTextWidget` lists `text-editor.js` before
  `text-editor-extras.js` in *both* of its appearances/contexts — there never
  was a conflicting order between those two files.
* The final combined order (`text-editor-extras.js, color-picker.js,
  text-editor.js`) actually violates the only real constraint that
  `FancyTextWidget.Media.js` states, namely that `text-editor.js` must come
  before `text-editor-extras.js` and before `color-picker.js`.

## What is wrong with `merge`'s approach

`Media.merge(list_1, list_2)` is a purely **pairwise, single-pass, greedy
list-splicing algorithm** — it is not a general topological sort of the
constraints implied by all the lists it has ever combined:

1. **It only ever looks at two lists at a time and immediately collapses them
   into one flat, ordered list.** All information about *why* an ordering
   holds (i.e. which original list demanded which relative order) is thrown
   away after each merge. When the third widget's list is merged in, the
   algorithm no longer knows that the current combined list's ordering
   (`color-picker.js` before `text-editor.js`) came from an earlier merge that
   involved widgets with no opinion about their relative order at all — it
   just treats `combined_list`'s current order as if it were an established
   constraint on par with a real one.

2. **The insertion algorithm is not a proper topological sort.** It walks
   `list_2` in reverse and inserts/repositions elements using a single
   `last_insert_index` cursor, which encodes only a "insert relative to the
   last thing I placed" heuristic, not the full set of pairwise ordering
   constraints from `list_2` (e.g. "text-editor.js before
   text-editor-extras.js" *and* "text-editor-extras.js before
   color-picker.js" *and* "text-editor.js before color-picker.js"). Because it
   never builds an explicit dependency graph and never checks it for
   consistency/cycles, it can (and does) silently produce final orderings
   that violate the constraints of the very Media list that provided the
   real order.

3. **The conflict warning is based on comparing positions in `combined_list`
   after other insertions have already reshuffled it, rather than comparing
   the original relative order that produced the constraint.** Because
   `color-picker.js` happened to precede `text-editor.js` in the combined
   list purely as an artifact of the merge order (an accidental relationship
   from a previous, order-agnostic merge, not a stated constraint), inserting
   `text-editor-extras.js` before `color-picker.js` (as `FancyTextWidget`
   demands, since `text-editor-extras.js` comes before `color-picker.js` in
   its list) makes `text-editor-extras.js` end up before `text-editor.js` too
   — triggering a warning that misattributes a conflict between
   `text-editor-extras.js` and `text-editor.js`, even though
   `FancyTextWidget.Media.js` orders those two consistently
   (`text-editor.js` before `text-editor-extras.js`) every time.

In short: `Media.merge` treats media-file ordering as a sequence of ad-hoc,
order-dependent pairwise list splices instead of collecting all the ordering
constraints from every widget's `Media` and computing a genuine topological
sort (e.g., via a dependency graph / Kahn's algorithm) over those constraints.
Because of this it can (a) falsely report an ordering conflict between two
files whose relative order was never actually contradicted, and (b) produce a
final combined order that violates a real ordering constraint stated by one
of the widgets, purely because of the arbitrary order in which the pairwise
merges happened to be performed.

results.finishSummary: Media.merge() in django/forms/widgets.py uses a naive pairwise, index-based list-merge (reverse-walk + last_insert_index) instead of building/solving real ordering constraints via something like a topological sort, so accidental orderings introduced by items unique to one list get treated as constraints in later merges, causing false MediaOrderConflictWarning and violating FancyTextWidget's actual declared order.

# Answer

## Responsible function

`django.forms.widgets.Media.merge()` (a `@staticmethod` on the `Media` class in
`django/forms/widgets.py`) is responsible for combining the `js`/`css` lists of
two `Media` objects into one ordered list. It is called repeatedly (pairwise,
via `Media.__add__`/`media_property`) to combine all the widgets' media
declarations when a `Form`'s combined `.media` property is built — that's how
`ColorPicker`, `SimpleTextWidget` and `FancyTextWidget`'s `js` lists end up
being merged two at a time.

## What is wrong with its approach

`merge(list_1, list_2)` is a purely **pairwise, positional/index-based**
algorithm. Given `list_1` and `list_2`, it:

1. starts `combined_list` as a copy of `list_1`,
2. walks `list_2` **in reverse**,
3. for each item:
   - if it isn't already in `combined_list`, inserts it at `last_insert_index`,
   - if it *is* already in `combined_list`, checks whether its existing
     index is *greater than* `last_insert_index` — if so, it emits a
     `MediaOrderConflictWarning` — and then sets `last_insert_index` to that
     item's index.

This procedure only ever looks at the *numeric position* of an item in the
partially-combined list compared to a single running cursor
(`last_insert_index`). It does **not** track the actual pairwise ordering
constraints ("A must come before B") that were explicitly stated within a
single widget's media list; instead it infers ordering purely from list
indices that shift around as items from *other* lists get spliced in between.

Concretely, for the example:

- `ColorPicker.Media.js = ['color-picker.js']`
- `SimpleTextWidget.Media.js = ['text-editor.js']`
- `FancyTextWidget.Media.js = ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`

When these get merged pairwise (e.g. merging `ColorPicker`'s `['color-picker.js']`
with `SimpleTextWidget`'s `['text-editor.js']` first produces
`['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']` because neither list constrains their
relative order — `merge` just appends what isn't present). Then merging that
result with `FancyTextWidget`'s `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js',
'color-picker.js']` finds `color-picker.js` sitting *before* `text-editor.js`
in the already-combined list (an artifact of the earlier, unconstrained
merge), even though `FancyTextWidget` itself never says `color-picker.js`
should precede `text-editor.js` — in `FancyTextWidget.Media.js`,
`text-editor.js` comes first and `color-picker.js` comes last. Because
`merge()` has already "baked in" the order `color-picker.js` before
`text-editor.js` from the first pairwise merge (a coincidental byproduct of
list concatenation, not an actual declared constraint), when it later
encounters `text-editor.js` and `text-editor-extras.js` from
`FancyTextWidget`, the bookkeeping via `last_insert_index` gets confused by
that stale, accidental ordering and reports `text-editor.js` and
`text-editor-extras.js` as being in conflicting order — even though every
single input list that mentions both of them (only `FancyTextWidget`) lists
them in exactly the same relative order (`text-editor.js` before
`text-editor-extras.js`).

The underlying bug is architectural: `Media.merge()` treats "media ordering"
as a series of two-list index/position merges (essentially a naive
positional interleave, similar to a diff/patience-style merge) rather than
building a proper dependency graph of "X must precede Y" constraints taken
from each *individual* widget's declared list and performing something like a
topological sort over the union of those constraints. Because ordering
information from one pairwise merge is discarded/flattened into a single
combined list before the next merge happens, transient, coincidental
orderings introduced by unconstrained items (items that appear in only one of
the two lists being merged, and are simply appended) get treated as real
constraints in later merges, producing both:

1. false-positive `MediaOrderConflictWarning`s (as with
   `text-editor.js`/`text-editor-extras.js` here), and
2. a final ordering that can actually violate a constraint explicitly given
   by one of the original `Media` classes (here, `FancyTextWidget` wants
   `text-editor.js, text-editor-extras.js, color-picker.js`, but merge can
   yield an order where `color-picker.js` precedes `text-editor.js`).

In short: `Media.merge()`'s two-list, index-based algorithm cannot correctly
preserve/aggregate ordering constraints across more than two lists/multiple
merges, because it conflates "no stated relationship between two items" with
"an actual ordering constraint" once concatenated into the combined list, and
it never considers all constraints together (e.g., via topological sort) to
find an order consistent with every widget's declared relative ordering.
